chapter_theme: Acuvakanthan's frightened counsellors urge that a small foe be put down before he grows, Arimanju counsels testing him first by a tribute demand, and the four envoys of the discus-bearer fly to Podanam, are admitted by the gatekeeper and deliver a letter demanding wealth, a thousand dancing women and the marks of a king.

cast.role: the rival king of the discus
the frightened counsellors who spoke before Arimanju, read as the rival king's
the counsellor who proposes testing the foe by a tribute demand
the four envoys of the discus-bearer sent to Podanam
the gatekeeper of the palace of Podanam
the reader who reads out the letter

643.reading: The speaker warns that a fire, however small its spark, blackens what it touches, and that a foe of old, though small, can win once he is allowed to spread.
643.nuance: The speakers are not named; they are read as the frightened ones whom verse 646 says spoke before Arimanju. The rival king is not named in the verse.

claims.claim: a small enemy left alone until he has spread can come to conquer

644.reading: The speaker says a poisonous thorny tree can be killed at the sprout, even with a nail, but once it has grown tall neither axe nor hatchet will master it.
644.nuance: The first line is compressed (the words for the poisonous thorn tree run together), and the sense of the second line is taken from the whole image.

claims.claim: an enemy must be uprooted while he is young, since once grown he cannot be cut down

645.reading: The speaker urges the king not to despise the foe as small but to go again and again and learn of him, a king with a honeyed garland and a crown of red gold.
645.nuance: The syntax is thin: whether the last line names the foe or only addresses the king is not fixed by the words, and it is read here as the foe.

claims.claim: a foe must not be scorned as small but must be known by going to see

646.reading: After the frightened speakers have spoken, a man named Arimanju says that if the foe proves truly an enemy, the king should first examine and see, and only then take counsel.
646.nuance: The name is read as Arimanju because the end of line 1 runs into it; the verse opens as the poet's link and passes into his speech.
646.event: Arimanju steps in after the frightened counsellors and urges the king to examine the foe before he plans against him.

claims.claim: a foe is to be tested and known before action is planned against him

647.reading: Arimanju says that making enemies of those who are not enemies, and counting as friends those of an ill heart, will both torment later through excess.
647.nuance: This sets Arimanju's caution against the counsellors' haste in 643 and 644. The word in line 2 for the ill-hearted one is corrupt and is read as the ill-hearted person.

claims.claim: making foes of the harmless and friends of the ill-minded both bring later pain

648.reading: Arimanju proposes to learn the foe's mind by sending to him for tribute: if he gives it in due order with courteous words, well; if he falls short, no fault will lie with the king.
648.nuance: The test is built to fail: a king who pays acknowledges the overlord, and one who does not has put himself in the wrong. The last line is compressed.

claims.claim: a demand for tribute is a fair test of a rival, and his refusal clears the demander of fault

649.reading: On hearing this the crowned king calls it good and sends messengers to the spear-bearing king with the order to take the tribute.
649.nuance: Neither king is named; the crowned king is read as Acuvakanthan and the spear-bearer as the king of Podanam, from the arrival in 651.
649.event: Acuvakanthan accepts Arimanju's plan and sends envoys to the victorious-spear king to demand tribute.

650.reading: Four envoys in bright dress, bearing letters pressed with an unbroken seal, set out together along a path through the clouds.
650.nuance: Several words in lines 1 and 3 are obscure (the ones for the red-lac staves and for their knowledge of the dance), so the description of the four is partly guessed.
650.event: Four envoys with sealed letters set out through the clouds.

651.reading: The envoys make for the southern quarter and its hills and, speaking on and on, enter the great city of Podanam that rises high.
651.event: The envoys enter the great city of Podanam.

652.reading: The mansions, lit like lightning among the clouds, block the sun's street, and seeing them the envoys turn in disgust from the wealth of their own Vidyadhara kind.
652.nuance: The envoys are taken as Vidyadharas because the verse speaks of the Vidyadhara wealth they leave behind; the verse does not call them so.
652.event: The envoys, seeing the mansions of Podanam, come to disdain the wealth of their own people.

653.reading: The swelling sound of drums, the peacocks that dance to it as to thunder and the festive streets give the envoys, as they pass, a glow of splendour.
653.nuance: The wording is dense and the last two lines are read only for their general sense, the subject of the verb for glory being supplied.

654.reading: Cascades fall from the clouds that the mansions' spire-tops cleave, and the envoys see the many streets of the city.
654.event: The envoys walk the streets of Podanam under mansion-cascades.

655.reading: The long streets lie covered with the gem girdles of lovers and the garlands flung by those in sulks, so that the envoys find passage hard.
655.nuance: The picture of lovers' quarrels is read from the words for the girdles and garlands; the sentence is long and compressed.
655.event: The envoys struggle to pass through streets strewn with ornaments.

656.reading: The street is mired with the rut and spittle of the great elephants, so that the envoys take it for a field of fragrant toddy-mad ground.
656.event: The envoys see the streets of rut-wet ground.

657.reading: The envoys come to the walled city that lies behind a rushing moat, where bees cluster on lilies and swans cry out.
657.event: The envoys reach the walled royal town.

658.reading: Standing before the palace gate with its high turrets, they speak to the guard.
658.event: The envoys, at the palace gate, address the guard.

659.reading: The envoys tell the gatekeeper to go before the king and say that the men of the bright discus-bearer, come from the silver ridge, stand at the gate.
659.nuance: The envoys name only their master's discus and do not name him; the ridge of silver is read as the Vidyadhara ridge.
659.event: The envoys have the gatekeeper announce them as the men of the discus-bearer.

660.reading: At their words the gatekeeper bows to the king's feet and tells him, and the king says that they may come in.
660.event: The gatekeeper reports the envoys, and the king bids them enter.

661.reading: The gatekeeper tells the envoys to come in, and they approach the king, bless his anklets and, with folded hands, give him the letter they had folded.
661.event: The envoys enter, bless the king and give him the folded letter.

662.reading: After the reader has read the letter before the king, the discus-king's men repeat in matching words what it says.
662.nuance: The last word (உரைத்தர்) is short of a syllable and the sense of line 3 is clipped; the verse is taken as a link to the demand in 663 to 665.
662.event: A reader reads the discus-king's letter aloud and his men repeat its demand.

663.reading: The speaker begins the list of what must be given: gleaming mansions by the thousand crore and a thousand dancing women with bangled arms and ear-rolls.
663.nuance: The sentence runs on through 664 and 665 and ends there. The word in line 2 for the first thing demanded is obscure, and 'mansions' is a guess.

664.reading: The list goes on: conches thrown up by the sea, coral, heaps of pearl, aloe wood, silk and the many goods that come with the waters.

665.reading: The list ends with white-rayed pearls, aloe, elephant tusks, whisks of white yak-hair and the cool white umbrella, all of which must be given, says the speech of the bright-discus king.
665.nuance: The white umbrella and the yak-hair whisks are the marks of a king, so the demand goes past tribute toward giving up his standing. The verse does not say Podanam yields or refuses.
665.event: The envoys finish reading the demand for wealth, women and royal insignia.

claims.claim: a lesser king owes an overlord, on demand, tribute of treasure, women and the marks of a king

links.note: Kural 674 says what is left over of a deed or a feud scorches like a fire's remnant; verse 643 draws the same fire but warns of a foe still small.
links.teaches: The epic's counsellors aim the couplet's fire at an enemy not yet seen to strike, which turns a rule about unfinished business into a case for striking first.

gains.a: The verse lacks the rule that an unfinished enmity is a remnant that will burn, which the couplet states as a general law.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a counsellor's use of it against a foe who has done nothing yet, which the verse supplies.

links.note: Kural 879 tells the king to cut a thorn tree young lest the hand that cuts it be hurt; verse 644 adds a nail for the sprout and that axe and hatchet fail once it has grown.
links.teaches: The verse makes the couplet's thorn tree an argument for haste, though Arimanju's reply in 646 to 648 shows the story doubts that the tree is a thorn at all.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's warning that the grown tree harms the hand that cuts it, a cost to the cutter and not only to the tree.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the image of tools failing, which makes the delay one of means as well as of danger.

links.note: Kural 871 says no one should want enmity even in jest; verse 647 says that making foes of the harmless and trusting the ill-hearted both burn later.
links.teaches: Arimanju's caution answers the counsellors' haste with the Kural's own rule against courting enmity, so the epic stages two readings of Kural 879 and 871 as rival counsel.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's reason that enmity has no good in it, and gives only its later pain.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the second warning, against counting the ill-hearted as friends, which the verse pairs with it.

links.note: Verse 304 says that kings of the earth, fearing the rival's anger, paid tribute and sent word; verses 663 to 665 show the same demand arriving at Podanam.
links.teaches: The tribute that 304 named as the rival's usual power is shown here in the act, and its list shows how much he asks of the one he treats as a vassal.

links.note: Verse 514 reads the Vidyadhara king's letter to the lord of Podanam, which sends gifts and good wishes; verse 662 reads the discus-king's letter to the same lord, which demands them.
links.teaches: A letter sealed and read at the same palace first carries a gift and a request and then a demand, so the same act of reading shows two different powers dealing with Podanam.

links.note: Kural 756 counts what falls to the king, customs and what he takes from crushed foes as his wealth; verse 665 lists treasure and royal marks demanded of a king who has not been crushed.
links.teaches: The epic shows the third kind of the couplet's royal wealth being claimed before any war, by an overlord's letter and not by victory.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule that foe-wealth is a king's by right, which would make the demand lawful as the speaker claims.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where such wealth is demanded by letter before any fight, and where the foe is asked to give up his own umbrella.

source_issues: Verse 647 line 2: the word for the ill-hearted one (தாமரை) looks corrupt.
Verse 662 line 4: the last word (உரைத்தர்) is short of a syllable.
Verses 650, 653 and 663: several words are obscure and the readings are partly guessed.
Verses 643 to 649: neither king is named; the rival is read as Acuvakanthan from verse 619 and the arrival at Podanam in 651.
